label: Integration on Manifolds
notes: This chapter, printed pages 400 to 439, builds the intrinsic theory of integration. The headline is that differential forms, not plain functions, are the natural integrands on an oriented manifold, and that exterior differentiation paired with the boundary operator yields Stokes's theorem, the grand generalization of every classical integral theorem.

label: Why Forms, Not Functions
notes: Open with the failure of naive integration. A scalar function has no coordinate-free integral on a manifold because the change-of-variables Jacobian appears uninvited. An n-form already carries that Jacobian determinant in its transformation law, so its integral is well defined. This is the motivating insight for the entire chapter.

label: The Signed Volume Meter
notes: Stress that an alternating top tensor measures signed volume of a tuple of tangent vectors as a determinant. Swapping two vectors flips the sign, and linearly dependent vectors give zero. This antisymmetry is exactly why the determinant, and hence orientation, enters the change-of-variables formula later.

label: Integrating Forms on Euclidean Space
notes: Define the integral of a compactly supported n-form on an open subset of R-n by erasing the wedge and integrating its single coefficient as an ordinary Lebesgue integral. This is the local building block; everything on a manifold is reduced to this Euclidean prototype through charts.

label: Change of Variables and Orientation
notes: Here is the linchpin. The pullback of a top form multiplies the substituted coefficient by the Jacobian determinant, not its absolute value. An orientation-preserving diffeomorphism leaves the integral unchanged, while an orientation-reversing one flips its sign. This is why integration of forms requires an orientation to be unambiguous.

label: Defining the Manifold Integral
notes: Assemble the global integral. Choose oriented charts, subordinate a partition of unity to the cover, integrate each chart-supported piece in its coordinate representation, and sum. Independence of the chart and partition choices follows from the orientation-respecting change-of-variables formula, so the manifold integral is genuinely well defined.

label: Partition of Unity Assembly
notes: Make the bookkeeping concrete. The partition functions are nonnegative, sum to one on the support of the form, and each rho-times-omega lives inside a single chart. The integral over the manifold is the sum of these local integrals, and the unity condition guarantees nothing is double counted or lost.

label: Manifolds with Boundary
notes: Introduce the induced orientation on the boundary. Using the outward-pointing normal first convention, an oriented manifold with boundary hands its boundary a canonical orientation. Getting this sign convention right is what makes the boundary integral in Stokes's theorem unambiguous and consistent with the classical results.

label: Stokes's Theorem
notes: State the centerpiece. For a smooth compactly supported n-minus-one form on an oriented n-manifold with boundary, the integral of d-omega over the manifold equals the integral of omega over the boundary with its induced orientation. Sketch the proof: reduce by partition of unity to a half-space and apply the fundamental theorem of calculus.

label: Stokes on a Region
notes: Visualize the two-dimensional case. Over a planar region the integral of d-omega equals the circulation of omega around the boundary curve. This is Green's theorem in disguise, and the picture of interior cancellation explains why only the outer boundary survives in the sum.

label: Classical Corollaries
notes: Show that the classics are special cases. The fundamental theorem of calculus is Stokes in dimension one, Green's theorem and the Kelvin-Stokes circulation theorem are the two-dimensional faces, and the divergence theorem is the flux form. One identity, d-omega over M equals omega over the boundary, contains them all.

label: Riemannian Integration
notes: Add a metric. An oriented Riemannian manifold carries a canonical volume form whose coordinate coefficient is the square root of the determinant of the metric. Integrating functions against this volume form recovers familiar surface area and volume, and the divergence theorem gains its metric flux interpretation.

label: Densities and Recap
notes: Close with densities, the absolute-value cousin of the volume form, which integrate even when orientation fails, as on the Mobius band. Recap the arc: forms integrate intrinsically, partitions assemble them, Stokes unifies the boundary, and metrics and densities extend the theory to measurement and to nonorientable spaces.
